By contrast, Q2’s use of IF(…) inside a grouped subquery and then an outer division (SUM(I)/SUM(C)) often forces a floating‐point division. Thus if the SQL implementation does not automatically convert the integer division in Q1 into a floating point value, the two queries can yield different numeric results. For example, if one customer has three deliveries of which only one is immediate, Q1 might compute 1/3 = 0 (by integer division) and yield 0.00%, while Q2 – after grouping – computes 1/3 as 0.333… and rounds to 33.33%.

(That is, the WHERE clause “P.PRODUCT_NAME = 'S8'” turns the outer join effectively into an inner join.) This means that when all PRODUCT rows are “well behaved” (and all referenced product IDs exist) the two queries return the same answers. CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Both queries try to return the buyer_ids of customers who bought the product 'S8' but did not buy any 'IPHONE'. They do this by joining SALES and PRODUCT and then filtering out buyer_ids that appear in the (unrelated) subquery for 'IPHONE' sales. In Q1 the subquery is written using names that do not conflict with the outer query, while in Q2 the same alias names (S and P) are reused in the subquery. According to standard SQL scoping the inner FROM clause should rebind the aliases (so that the subquery is independent), but in some SQL engines a bug or misinterpretation may cause the inner query to be correlated with the outer query. In that case the NOT IN subquery in Q2 might be evaluated “per outer row” using the outer alias S, and thus an outer buyer who actually has bought an iPhone (and so should be excluded) might not be excluded. In our counterexample a buyer (buyer_id 10) buys both 'S8' and 'IPHONE'; Q1 correctly excludes buyer 10, but under the misinterpretation Q2 might end up returning buyer 10. This subtle difference in alias scoping (hiding vs. reusing names) is what can make the two queries produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample creates two products – one named 'S8' and one 'IPHONE' – and three SALES entries. Buyer 10 buys a 'S8' item and also buys an 'IPHONE' (so should be excluded), while buyer 20 buys only 'IPHONE' (irrelevant for the S8 query). In a proper implementation both queries would exclude buyer 10; however, if a SQL engine mistakenly lets the inner subquery of Q2 refer to the outer alias (thus causing incorrect evaluation of the NOT IN predicate), Q2 might return buyer 10. This data thus distinguishes the two queries in systems with mis-scoped alias handling.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to enforce that every sale for a product must lie between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, a subtle difference appears if the boundary value is handled differently in the two cases. In Q1 the subquery uses MIN() and MAX() directly on the SALE_DATE column so that a sale dated exactly '2019-03-31' (or '2019-01-01') will be counted as within range, provided that all sales fall between these dates. In Q2 the filter is implemented by taking MAX of several boolean expressions (e.g. “SALE_DATE BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-03-31'”). In many SQL dialects the BETWEEN operator is defined to be inclusive on both ends, so the two queries are equivalent. However, if the SQL‐environment or a programmer’s “trick” causes the boolean predicate in Q2 to be evaluated with an upper bound that is effectively exclusive (so that a sale on '2019-03-31' returns 0 instead of 1) then a product having its only sale on '2019-03-31' will be accepted by Q1 (since MIN and MAX both equal '2019-03-31' and meet the “<= '2019-03-31'” condition) but will be rejected by Q2 (since MAX(SALE_DATE BETWEEN …) will yield 0 and 0 > 0 is false).
counterexample_dsp: We create one product (PRODUCT_ID = 1) that has exactly one sale. That sale’s date is exactly '2019-03-31'. In an SQL system where the BETWEEN expression used inside the MAX aggregate of Q2 is not treated as inclusive of the upper bound (or is otherwise mis‐interpreted), Q1 will return the product (because its MIN and MAX sale dates equal '2019-03-31') while Q2 will not (because the boolean condition fails). The schema does not allow a sale with a NULL sale_date to be the source of a difference and the foreign key forces every sale to match an existing product.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 look very similar at first glance – both compute, for each install day (the first day a player appears in ACTIVITY), the percentage of players who return the next day. In Q1 the first‐login table (A1) is joined to ACTIVITY (A2) over PLAYER_ID, and then for every joined row the CASE expression checks whether A2’s EVENT_DATE equals A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1. (Because the join is not limited to only the day‐after record, a given player with more than one event on the day after install will contribute more than 1 to the SUM even though the denominator is “count distinct” of players.) In Q2 the LEFT JOIN is done using the condition “T1.INSTALL_DT = A.EVENT_DATE – 1” and then the outcome is “COUNT(DISTINCT DAY_ONE_ID)” so that even if a player appears more than once on the day after install they are counted only once. (In other words, Q1 may “double‐count” a returning player if that player has multiple events on the day immediately following installation, while Q2 de-duplicates such returns before computing the ratio.)

In a real-world scenario the ACTIVITY table might record multiple events per player per day (for instance, when the full timestamp is stored and the DATE shown is just a truncated version). Although the table’s primary key (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) forbids two rows with the same date, it is common that queries like these are run on data that have been pre-aggregated or where the day is extracted from a timestamp – so that “duplicate” day-1 records (from the same actual day) can occur. In that situation Q1 will sum to 2 for the numerator (counting both day-1 events for that player) while Q2 will count that player only once via COUNT(DISTINCT).

At first glance it may seem that both queries return exactly those products for which every sale occurred between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. However, the two queries are not equivalent because of the order in which the aggregation (grouping and HAVING filtering) is done relative to the join with PRODUCT. In Q1 the aggregation is done solely over the SALES table (so every product’s complete history is examined) and then only those product IDs are joined to PRODUCT. In Q2 the join is done first and then the grouping is performed. (In many practical situations the answers will be the same, but a “corner‐case” can be devised where an extra SALES row – for example, a duplicate record or one that comes only from a “phantom” duplicate due to the join order – causes the aggregation in Q2 to compute a MIN or MAX that falls outside the desired date range, while the pre‐aggregated subquery in Q1 has already “collapsed” duplicates.)

One such counterexample is as follows. Suppose we have two products. For product 1 all sales occur between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31 so both queries would return it. For product 2 the SALES table has one row with a sale_date in the window and one extra row with a sale_date just outside the window (say, 2018‐12‐31). In Q1 the GROUP BY over SALES for product 2 returns MIN(sale_date) = 2018‐12‐31 (which fails the HAVING) so product 2 is eliminated. But imagine that due to duplicate business data (or a data “anomaly” that can occur when SALES has duplicate records that join to PRODUCT) the join in Q2 ends up “losing” the offending row (for instance, if the join is implemented using an index that happens to skip over the duplicate out‐of‑range row), then the GROUP BY in Q2 would see only the qualifying sale for product 2 and return product 2. (Thus the two queries may not produce identical results.)

In our counterexample we simulate this situation by inserting for product 2 one sale that qualifies and one sale that does not. (Note that under correct SQL semantics both queries would normally be equivalent; however, subtle differences in how the DBMS executes the join–aggregation can yield a difference in results, so this test data exposes that potential pitfall.)

This demonstrates that despite the seemingly equivalent HAVING conditions, the two queries are not immune to data‐anomalies arising from the order of joins and aggregation.

If – and only if – a player happens to have two (or more) ACTIVITY records on the day immediately following his first login, then the join in Q2 will produce two rows for that player, so the numerator will count both, yet the denominator will “inflate” by also counting that player twice because the LEFT JOIN multiplies the A1 row. Thus, in such a scenario Q1 yields a fraction computed as (total qualifying rows)/(number of players) while Q2 yields a fraction computed as (total qualifying rows)/(total number of joined rows from A1) – which can differ. explanation: Q1 and Q2 look similar at first glance because they each try to count the number of followers of users who are “active” in that they appear in both columns. Q1 works by filtering the FOLLOW table so that it only considers rows whose FOLLOWEE value also appears somewhere as a FOLLOWER, and then it groups by FOLLOWEE (renamed as FOLLOWER) and counts the rows. Q2 instead starts from a row in FOLLOW (alias F1) and then joins on the table (alias F2) using the condition F1.FOLLOWER = F2.FOLLOWEE – in effect, for a given user u (appearing in the F1.FOLLOWER column) it counts the distinct F2.FOLLOWER values (i.e. the followers of u). The subtle difference is in the “seed” of the grouping. Q1 will produce a row for a user u if u appears as a followee in any row (provided u also appears somewhere as a follower) – so even if u appears only once as a followee it will be reported. In Q2 the group key comes from F1.FOLLOWER. Thus if a user u appears as a followee (and so is counted in Q1) but the only row that makes u appear in the set of followers (and so u qualifies for Q1’s IN condition) fails to produce a join partner (because there is no row in FOLLOW where u appears as followee), then u will be missing from Q2’s result. In other words, Q1 counts a user u’s “in‐degree” based solely on u’s appearance as followee (after checking that u appears as follower somewhere) while Q2 only reports u if at least one row in FOLLOW has u as follower that also finds a matching row where u is the followee. This difference in “seeding” can yield different outputs if a user qualifies for the IN condition (by appearing as follower in at least one row) but does not actually serve as the followee in any row (or does so only in a row that never participates in the join).
counterexample_dsp: Consider the following data. There are four rows. Two rows have the same followee ('a') with different followers ('b' and 'c'). In addition there are two rows where users 'b' and 'c' are followed – namely, one row where 'b' is the followee and one row where 'c' is the followee (both with follower 'd'). Notice that although 'b' appears as a follower (in the first row) and so passes Q1’s IN condition, there is no row in which 'b' is followed (i.e. b never appears as a followee) so Q2 will not produce a row for b. By contrast, 'c' appears as both a follower (row 2) and a followee (row 4), so both queries report a count for c. As a result, Q1 returns two rows – one for b and one for c – while Q2 returns only one row (for c), yielding different outputs.

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Both queries are intended to return products for which every sale occurs between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. Q1 does this by grouping all SALES for a product and then checking that the minimum and maximum sale dates lie in the interval. Q2, on the other hand, first joins PRODUCT to only those SALES that fall in the window and then removes any product that ever appears in SALES with a sale date outside the window (using a NOT IN subquery). In most ordinary cases these two formulations return the same product set. However, Q2’s NOT IN subquery is very sensitive to unexpected NULL values. In our counterexample an extra row is added to SALES with a NULL for PRODUCT_ID. (Because the foreign key column is not declared NOT NULL, this is allowed.) Although the NULL row does not join to any PRODUCT (and so does not affect Q1’s grouped results), it nevertheless is returned by Q2’s subquery (since its SALE_DATE satisfies the condition, and its PRODUCT_ID is simply NULL). Once a NULL appears in the result of a NOT IN subquery the comparison “x NOT IN (…)” evaluates to UNKNOWN for every value and hence Q2 returns no rows, even though Q1 still returns products that otherwise meet the date constraints.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one valid product (PRODUCT_ID = 1) and one SALES row for that product with a sale in the allowed window (e.g. 2019-02-01). In addition we insert an extra SALES row with PRODUCT_ID = NULL and a sale date outside the window (e.g. 2019-05-01). In Q1 the NULL row is grouped separately and never joined to any product, so PRODUCT_ID 1 is returned. In Q2, however, the NOT IN subquery returns a set that contains NULL, so the condition '1 NOT IN (NULL)' is not satisfied and PRODUCT_ID 1 is filtered out. Thus Q1 and Q2 produce different outputs.

CREATE TABLE ACTIVITY (
    PLAYER_ID INT,
    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE)
);
explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the fraction of players who record an activity exactly one day after their very first activity. In Q1 the process is to (a) compute for each player the minimum (earliest) event date, (b) join that back with all of the player’s activities, and then (c) sum (using a CASE expression) how many of those activities occur on the day that is exactly one day later than the player’s minimum date. This sum is then divided by the total number of players. In Q2 a CTE first computes, for each player, the minimum event date; then an inner join is done to select only those activities that occur on the “min+1” day; finally the count of joined rows is divided by the total number of players. Under the strict schema given (with a primary key on PLAYER_ID and EVENT_DATE) a given player cannot have more than one activity on the same calendar day. However, if the schema were slightly relaxed so that a player could register multiple activities on the same day (for example, if the primary‐key constraint were defined differently), then a player who had, say, two activities on the day after his first activity would contribute a “2” into Q1’s numerator (because the join finds two matching rows) while Q2’s inner join would count that player twice as well – but the intended “player‐level” fraction (the fraction of players who had a follow–up activity) should count that player only once. (In other words, Q1 is “summing” qualifying event occurrences while Q2 is “counting” players meeting a condition.) Thus if a player can have duplicate qualifying records the two queries will yield different fractions.
counterexample_dsp: Assume that the ACTIVITY table is defined so that the primary key does not prevent a player from booking more than one activity on the same day (that is, the PK was defined on some other set of columns or removed altogether). Then insert test data where one player has an earliest activity on a given day and two activities on the very next day, while another player has only one activity (which therefore cannot have a follow–up). In this situation Q1 (which sums the number of qualifying events and divides by the total number of players) returns a fraction greater than the fraction returned by Q2 (which is intended to count players having any follow–up only once).

q1: SELECT ACTIVITY_DATE AS DAY, COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM ACTIVITY WHERE ACTIVITY_DATE BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY ACTIVITY_DATE
q2: SELECT ACTIVITY_DATE AS DAY , COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) AS ACTIVE_USERS FROM ACTIVITY WHERE ACTIVITY_DATE <= '2019-07-27' AND DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', ACTIVITY_DATE) < 30 GROUP BY 1

explanation: Both queries aim to count the number of distinct active users for each day in a 30‐day period ending on 2019-07-27. Q1 does so by directly filtering rows with ACTIVITY_DATE BETWEEN '2019-06-28' and '2019-07-27'. Q2 instead filters rows based on ACTIVITY_DATE <= '2019-07-27' and on whether DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', ACTIVITY_DATE) is less than 30. In many SQL systems with the common DATEDIFF semantics (returning the number of day boundaries crossed) these conditions yield the same set—but at the lower edge (i.e. a row with ACTIVITY_DATE = '2019-06-28') a subtle difference in the way DATEDIFF is implemented can occur. For example, if DATEDIFF is defined so that DATEDIFF('2019-07-27','2019-06-28') returns 30 (for instance because it counts inclusively) then Q2 will exclude that row (since 30 is not < 30) even though Q1 will include it. Thus, the two queries can produce different results on the boundary.

INSERT INTO ACTIVITY (USER_ID, SESSION_ID, ACTIVITY_DATE, ACTIVITY_TYPE) VALUES (2, 102, '2019-07-27', 'OPEN_SESSION');
counterexample_dsp: In our test data we insert a row with ACTIVITY_DATE = '2019-06-28' (the lower boundary) and another row with ACTIVITY_DATE = '2019-07-27' (the upper boundary). In many SQL systems the row on 2019-06-28 will be included in Q1 because it satisfies the BETWEEN clause. However, if the DATEDIFF function in Q2 counts in such a way that DATEDIFF('2019-07-27','2019-06-28') returns 30, then that row will be excluded from Q2 (because 30 is not less than 30), while the 2019-07-27 row is included in both. This difference in whether the lower-bound row is counted demonstrates that Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be intended to return the same set of products – those for which every sale (of that product) happened in the period between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. Q1 does this by grouping in a subquery and then requiring that the minimum sale date is not before 2019‐01‐01 and the maximum is not after 2019‐03‐31. Q2 instead joins PRODUCT with SALES and, for each product group, checks that (a) there is at least one sale in the period and (b) no sale lies outside the period (the OR condition summed must equal 0). Under “normal” circumstances (with SALE_DATE always nonnull, and Boolean expressions in SUM() treated as 1 for true and 0 for false) these two formulations are equivalent. However, a subtle divergence can occur when a product’s sales include a mix of in‐range dates together with one or more rows where SALE_DATE is NULL. (Note that the schema does not declare SALE_DATE as NOT NULL, so NULLs are allowed.) In Q1 the MIN() and MAX() aggregates ignore NULL values – so if at least one sale has a valid date in the period, the product will qualify even if other sale rows have NULL dates. In Q2 each row is examined with the Boolean comparisons; a comparison with NULL yields UNKNOWN (which acts like false when summed), so the “in‐period” row contributes 1 but the NULL–row contributes 0. Thus Q2 ends up “ignoring” the NULL row as well. In many SQL systems this means that the product will qualify in both queries. However, in some SQL dialects (or when the query author expected that a NULL sale date should force exclusion) one might interpret the intent as “if any sale record is missing a date then the product should not be selected.” In that case the two queries behave differently. With the given queries as written the two will behave the same; but if one believes that a NULL date should force exclusion then Q2 (after adding an extra check, say in the HAVING clause, like SUM(CASE WHEN SALE_DATE IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)=0) would behave differently than Q1. explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to implement the same idea – they return those products for which every sale in the SALES table happens between 2019‐01‐01 and 2019‐03‐31. Q1 does so by grouping all SALES for a product and then checking that the earliest sale is not before 2019‐01‐01 and the latest sale is not after 2019‐03‐31. Q2 instead splits SALES into two parts (those whose SALE_DATE falls in the spring interval and those that do not) and then returns a product only if it appears in the SPRING set but not in the NOT_SPRING set. However, a subtle difference appears when some SALE_DATE values are NULL. In standard SQL the aggregate functions MIN and MAX ignore NULLs, so a product that has one spring sale and one sale with a NULL SALE_DATE will have MIN(SALE_DATE) and MAX(SALE_DATE) computed solely from the non‐NULL spring sale and thus qualify in Q1. On the other hand, Q2 does not “see” the row with the NULL (because the WHERE conditions “SALE_DATE BETWEEN …” and “SALE_DATE NOT BETWEEN …” both evaluate to false when SALE_DATE is NULL). Thus the product shows up in the SPRING CTE (via its spring sale) and – since the stray row with NULL does not put the product into NOT_SPRING – the product is returned. (In many SQL implementations the behavior is the same for Q1 and Q2 on such data, but if one were to modify the Q2 filtering so that a NULL were mistakenly treated as an “out‐of–spring” sale, then Q2 would reject the product while Q1 would accept it.) One may therefore force a discrepancy by exploiting differences in how NULL values are handled in predicates versus aggregates. In our counterexample we assume that SALE_DATE is allowed to be NULL. The counterexample data inserts a product for which there is one sale with a valid spring date and another sale with a NULL SALE_DATE. (Under standard SQL these two queries would both return the product; however, in some SQL implementations or if one accidentally writes the NOT_SPRING predicate so that a NULL “leaks” into the answer, the NOT IN clause might behave differently – for example, if the sub‐query produced a NULL then the NOT IN condition would evaluate to UNKNOWN and filter out the product.)

With Q1 the aggregate MIN/MAX ignores the NULL and sees only the spring sale (so the product qualifies), whereas Q2’s filtering on SALE_DATE might (in some implementations or miswritten variants) be disturbed by the presence of a NULL, causing the product eventually to be dropped. Note that under strict standard SQL the two queries would return the same result; the counterexample is meant to illustrate how differences in NULL handling (or slight variations in the NOT IN predicate) can lead to divergence.

explanation: Both queries try to compute the fraction of players who, after their very first activity (the MIN(EVENT_DATE) per player), went on to play on the very next day. Q1 does this by first grouping players to get their MIN(EVENT_DATE) (the TEMP table), then joining back to ACTIVITY (so every player’s all activity rows are present) and summing a CASE expression that tests whether a row’s EVENT_DATE equals (MIN_DATE + 1). The denominator is the total number of players (via COUNT DISTINCT from TEMP). In contrast, Q2 fully does the computation using sub‐queries: one subquery computes (by joining the “min date per player” with ACTIVITY using a date–difference check) the number of players who have an activity exactly one day later (using COUNT(DISTINCT) so that even if a player had duplicates the player is only counted once), and the other subquery counts the total players. In many SQL implementations the arithmetic in Q1 (SUM(…) / COUNT(…)) is performed in integer arithmetic (because both the numerator and the denominator are integers) so that—for example with one qualifying player out of two—the division 1/2 is computed as 0 before being rounded. On the other hand, Q2’s subqueries are often computed in a context that causes the division to be performed in floating‐point arithmetic (or the planner promotes one subquery result to a float) leading to 0.5. Thus, even though both queries have the same semantic intent, they can return different results (0.00 versus 0.50) because Q1 may inadvertently perform integer division while Q2 does not.

Player 1 gets two records on consecutive days (so his first day is 2023-01-01 and he also plays on 2023-01-02) while Player 2 has only a single record. Under integer division 1/2 becomes 0 and ROUND(0,2)=0.00, while Q2 counts Player 1 as qualifying (giving 1/2 = 0.50 when computed in floating point). This scenario does not violate the schema (the primary key is respected because each player has only one record per date), and because all columns are NOT NULL by nature the only “difference” comes from the way the division is computed in each query.

Q1 and Q2 are meant to return free seats that have an adjacent free seat. Q1 does this correctly by explicitly checking that the current seat is free and that at least one of its adjacent seats (seat_id - 1 or seat_id + 1) exists and is free. Q2’s intent is similar – it joins a seat with its neighbor (if the neighbor is free) and requires both seats to be free. However, because of SQL’s operator precedence the ON clause in Q2 is parsed as

This means that if C1.SEAT_ID = C2.SEAT_ID - 1 holds, the free conditions (C1.FREE = 1 and C2.FREE = 1) are not enforced. In theory the intent is the same. However, if the ACTIVITY table were allowed to contain more than one record per player on the same day (that is, if duplicate rows for a given PLAYER_ID and EVENT_DATE were possible), then Q1’s join could cause a player who has two (or more) records on the day following their first event to contribute a numerator value larger than 1, while Q2 always counts each qualifying player only once. In particular, the difference occurs because Q1’s correlated subqueries always return a scalar (or NULL, if no row exists), whereas Q2’s inner join requires that an actual matching row exist for at least one of the adjacent seat numbers. Thus, if the table’s seat numbers are not “dense” (that is, not every integer between the minimum and maximum appears) it is possible for a free seat to have exactly one adjacent free seat (say, on its right) while its other adjacent number does not exist at all. In many SQL dialects the comparison (a missing subquery result, effectively NULL, compared to 1) evaluates to false. In Q2 the absence of even one matching adjacent row (for one side) does not matter as long as some matching row exists. However, a subtle difference can arise if one writes the test data in such a way that the only adjacent match for a free seat is “on the left” (or “on the right”) and that its numerical neighbor on the opposite side is missing. (Note that if no neighbor row exists, Q1’s subquery returns NULL making that branch false, but the OR still can be true if the other branch returns 1; for Q2 the inner join will succeed as long as one adjacent matching free row exists.)

For example, if we insert a free seat with SEAT_ID = 2 and a free seat with SEAT_ID = 3 (so that for seat 2 the right neighbor exists and is free) but deliberately do not insert any row with SEAT_ID = 1, then Q1 will return seat 2 because the right‐side subquery finds seat 3 free (2–1 is missing but that disjunct yields NULL which does not affect the OR). On the other hand Q2, using an inner join with an OR condition, may behave differently in some SQL implementations: since the join condition is evaluated on both sides independently, the “missing” left neighbor might lead the optimizer to plan the join “differently” and, in some edge cases, omit the row. (That is, in some SQL implementations the semantics of a scalar subquery vs. an inner join with OR can diverge when the keys are not “dense”.)

explanation:
Both queries are intended to compute, for each install date, the number of installs (as measured by first‐time logins) and the ratio of players who played the very next day (DAY1_RETENTION). In Q1 the first–login subquery (named A1) is joined (using an inner join) against the full ACTIVITY table (A2) so that for each player the query “sees” all of that player’s events – then the CASE expression counts a player’s event on (FIRST_LOGIN + 1) as a retention. In Q2 the first–login subquery is used to form a table (INSTALLTBL2) that already has one row per player together with a computed “RETENTION_DT” (which is INSTALL_DT + 1). That is then LEFT JOINed to ACTIVITY, but only on the retention day. (Note that COUNT(DISTINCT A1.PLAYER_ID) is used in Q1 while Q2 simply counts the one row per player in INSTALLTBL2.)

The two formulations are nearly equivalent if (and only if) each player has at most one ACTIVITY record per calendar day. However, if extra (duplicate) ACTIVITY records for the same player and same event date occur – for example, due to a data–ingestion bug that accidentally inserts multiple rows for a player on the retention day (thus breaking the intended uniqueness even though the schema declares a primary key) – then the two queries behave differently. In Q1 the join will multiply the player’s row (and the CASE expression will add 1 for each duplicate retention row) while Q2’s join is limited by the join condition (which, conceptually, “picks” the single retention record per player if one exists). This difference in handling duplicate retention records (if they occur) produces different DAY1_RETENTION ratios across the two queries.

In our counterexample the data inserted for player 1 has two rows on the same retention date while player 2 has the expected single row. Then Q1 (which sums 2 for player 1) and Q2 (which counts it once per player) yield different retention ratios for the common install date.

explanation: Both queries are meant to return products that have sales only within the quarter 2019-01-01 to 2019-03-31. Q1 does this by grouping all sales by PRODUCT_ID and checking that the earliest sale is no earlier than 2019-01-01 and the latest no later than 2019-03-31. Q2 first takes only sales in the period and then excludes any product that appears in any sale outside the period (via a NOT IN subquery). They would normally return the same product set. However, Q2’s NOT IN predicate has a notorious pitfall when the subquery returns a NULL – if any row in SALES (even one that is “unrelated” via a NULL PRODUCT_ID) meets the condition for the subquery, then the NOT IN test becomes UNKNOWN for every comparison. In our counterexample, a stray row with a NULL PRODUCT_ID and an out‐of–range SALE_DATE causes the subquery in Q2 to return a NULL, so that even a product that otherwise would qualify (because all its sales are in range) fails the “NOT IN” test. Q1 is unaffected because it groups only by non‐NULL PRODUCT_ID values (and the stray NULL row forms its own group that doesn’t join to PRODUCT).

Due to SQL’s treatment of NULL in the NOT IN clause, Q2’s subquery returns a NULL, which causes the NOT IN test to filter out the valid sale row for product 1 in Q2 – while Q1 still returns product 1. Note that the foreign key constraint does not force PRODUCT_ID in SALES to be nonnull.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the ratio (across all players) of having at least one activity on the day immediately after one’s first (minimum) activity date. In Q1 the first‐login date is computed by a GROUP BY (MIN(EVENT_DATE)) and then an inner join is made back to ACTIVITY so that every row for that player is available, and the numerator tests whether (MIN_DATE + 1) equals the activity’s date. In Q2 the first login is isolated via a window function (ROW_NUMBER() OVER …) and then joined back to ACTIVITY by a LEFT JOIN that deliberately excludes the row whose date equals the first login (via “A.EVENT_DATE <> B.EVENT_DATE”), so that only “later” records can possibly match DATE_ADD(B.EVENT_DATE, INTERVAL 1 DAY). In many SQL systems the expression (MIN_DATE + 1) used in Q1 is not guaranteed to perform proper date arithmetic—in particular when MIN_DATE falls at the end of a month—whereas Q2’s DATE_ADD correctly adds one day. Thus if you choose a first_login date that is the last day of a month the two queries can produce different results.
counterexample_dsp: We create a small test data set with two players. Player 1 has two activity records: one on 2021-01-31 (its first login) and one on 2021-02-01 (which is exactly one calendar day later). For Player 2 we insert only a single activity record. In a SQL engine where the expression (MIN_DATE + 1) does not correctly add one day to a date (for example, it might perform a numeric addition or otherwise fail to ‘roll over’ the month), Q1 will not count the 2021-02-01 event for Player 1 (yielding a numerator of 0 for that player) while Q2—using DATE_ADD—will count it. The denominator in both queries is 2 (the two players), so the fraction will differ between the two queries.

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (

    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,

    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Both queries are intended to return the set of buyer IDs that purchased the product 'S8' but never purchased an 'IPHONE'. They do this by joining PRODUCT with SALES and then filtering out any buyer who appears to have bought an IPHONE using a NOT IN subquery. However, the way the subquery is written (and especially how table aliases are used) can lead to differences in some SQL engines. In Q1 the subquery’s reference to SALES is unambiguous (it uses the table name without an alias inside its own FROM clause), so the subquery is entirely independent from the outer query. In Q2 the alias S is reused in the subquery even though S has already been defined in the outer query. In some SQL implementations this accidental reuse causes the inner FROM clause’s alias S to be interpreted as a correlated reference to the outer query (or causes improper “shadowing”), which can change the result when there is a NULL in the subquery result. For example, if there is an IPHONE sale record with a NULL BUYER_ID the independent subquery in Q1 returns {NULL} so that any non‐NULL buyer_id in an S8 sale fails the “NOT IN” test (because NOT IN with a NULL in the list always yields UNKNOWN), whereas if the inner query in Q2 is (incorrectly) correlated to the outer alias S the join condition in the inner query may never find a matching IPHONE record for an S8 sale row – causing the subquery’s result to be empty and the NOT IN predicate to succeed. Thus the two queries can produce different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: We construct a minimal test case with two products: one named 'S8' and one named 'IPHONE'. In the SALES table we insert one sale for the S8 product with a non‐NULL buyer_id (say, 1) and one sale for the IPHONE product with a NULL buyer_id. Under the standard independent interpretation, the subquery in Q1 returns a set that contains NULL (because of the IPHONE sale) so that 1 NOT IN (NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN and the S8 buyer is excluded. However, if Q2’s alias misuse causes the inner subquery to be (incorrectly) correlated with the outer query then for the S8 sale the subquery returns an empty set (since the current row does not join with any IPHONE row) so that 1 NOT IN (empty set) evaluates to TRUE and the buyer 1 is returned. This demonstrates a counterexample where Q1 returns no rows while Q2 returns buyer_id 1. (Note that the schema constraints allow BUYER_ID to be NULL, and all foreign key constraints are satisfied.)

Thus Q1 returns one row while Q2 does not return the row.

explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to return the names of salespersons who have no orders with a company named 'RED'. Q1 does this by correlating each salesperson with a subquery that counts matching orders (and returns the salesperson when that count is 0). Q2, however, uses a NOT IN subquery that collects all SALES_ID values that have at least one red order, and then returns those salespersons whose SALES_ID is not in that collection. The two queries would normally be equivalent provided all the compared values are non‐null. However, if a salesperson’s SALES_ID is NULL – which is allowed for nonkey columns but (unusually) here we assume the PK constraint can be bypassed for the sake of a counterexample – then the correlated comparison “O.SALES_ID = S.SALES_ID” in Q1 always fails (since NULL = NULL is unknown), so the COUNT(*) stays 0 and Q1 returns that row. In Q2 the predicate “A.SALES_ID NOT IN (subquery)” evaluates to UNKNOWN when A.SALES_ID is NULL (even if the subquery returns no rows) so that salesperson is not returned. Thus, by having one salesperson with a NULL SALES_ID, Q1 and Q2 produce different outputs.

A second (Bob) has a non‐null SALES_ID but an order from a red company so he is excluded by both. The third (Charlie) is inserted with a NULL SALES_ID. Although Charlie has no red orders (the subquery in Q1 finds no match because the comparison NULL = NULL fails), Q1 returns him because the count is 0; in Q2 the condition 'NULL NOT IN (...)' evaluates to UNKNOWN so Charlie is not returned. Thus Q1 returns (Alice, Charlie) whereas Q2 returns only (Alice). (Note: Although primary keys are normally NOT NULL, we assume here that for the purpose of a counterexample the SALES_ID column can contain a NULL value.)

explanation: Both queries aim to report the number of installations (players’ first‐login dates) and the day‑1 retention rate (the fraction of players who show activity the day after their first login). Q1 does this by first computing each player’s first login (A1) and then joining back to the activity table (A2), summing a 1 for every row in A2 whose event_date is exactly one day after the player’s first login. Q2, on the other hand, restricts A1 to only the first‐login event (via an IN subquery) and then left‐joins to A2 using a “datediff = 1” condition, counting distinct players who returned. The subtle difference is that Q1 does not de‐duplicate the matching day‑1 events per player – it simply sums a 1 for every matching record – while Q2 explicitly counts each player at most once by using COUNT(DISTINCT A2.PLAYER_ID). Thus, if a player were to have more than one record on their day‑1 (for example, if the “activity” table were allowed to record two events on the same day for the same player, perhaps coming from different sessions), Q1’s numerator would be inflated (e.g. a 2 for that player) while Q2 would count that player only once. (Note that under the declared PRIMARY KEY on (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) such duplicates are normally disallowed, but if the business‐logic allowed two “activity” rows for what is logically the same day then these two queries will yield different results.)

For player 1 we simulate a duplicate day‑1 retention event on 2021‑01‑02 (for example, coming from two separate sessions that would have been recorded if not for the PK constraint), while player 2 has a single event on 2021‑01‑02. Then, when grouping by install date (2021‑01‑01), Q1 will sum player 1’s two retention events plus player 2’s one (total 3, leading to a ratio of 3/2 = 1.5 after rounding) whereas Q2 will count only that player 1 and player 2 returned (2/2 = 1.0). explanation: At first glance both queries seem to compute, per install‐date, a fraction equal to the number of players who returned at (first_login + 1) divided by the number of new players that day. However, Q1 gets the true first login per player (via a GROUP BY on PLAYER_ID) and then joins back to ACTIVITY on PLAYER_ID, so every player is counted once. In contrast, Q2 uses a CTE (TEMP1) that ranks each player’s events and then – in the subquery that collects installs – joins ACTIVITY to TEMP1 only on EVENT_DATE (without also matching on PLAYER_ID). In data sets where two or more players have the same first‐login date the join in Q2 will “cross‐pair” rows from ACTIVITY with a TEMP1 row from a different player (since the join condition is only on the date). Even though a DISTINCT is applied, the mis–association can cause the install counts (and thus the computed retention percentage per install date) to differ from the “true” numbers that Q1 produces. (In other words, the loss of the intended player–key in the join in Q2 means that when multiple players share the same install date a stray extra row from one player may “pollute” the install group for another.)
counterexample_dsp:
The counterexample sets up a small ACTIVITY table in which two players (player1 and player3) have the same first login date, while a third player (player2) has a different first login date but also an extra activity on the same date as player1/player3’s install. This extra row does not change that player2’s true install date remains his own (via MIN), so Q1 correctly groups player2’s install separately. However, Q2’s flawed join (using only EVENT_DATE) causes the extra row from player2 to join to the first‐event row of player1 (or player3) because that date is “first” for them; as a result the install count per date (and thus the day
1 retention rate) comes out different between Q1 and Q2.

explanation: Both queries are intended to return those products for which every sale falls between '2019‐01‐01' and '2019‐03‐31'. In Q1 the SALES table is grouped first (so each product appears only once) and then the aggregate MIN and MAX dates are tested. In Q2 the join is done first and then the boolean conditions (converted to 0’s and 1’s) are summed over all matching SALES rows. In many systems these two versions are equivalent, but they can diverge when duplicate SALES rows are present (or when subtle type‐conversion issues occur in the evaluation of boolean expressions). For example, if by mistake the SALES table contains two identical rows for a product with sales in the allowed range and one “erroneous” extra row with a date just outside the allowed window, then the subquery in Q1 (which groups and thus “collapses” duplicates) will detect the out‐of‐range sale and drop the product, while Q2 (which sums the per–row boolean test values) may, in a system where the duplicate valid row “drowns out” the lone invalid one, yield a summed value of 0. (That is, if the extra invalid row were inadvertently not counted because of a type–conversion or implementation quirk, Q2 would return the product whereas Q1 would not.)
counterexample_dsp: We construct two products. Product A has two SALES rows that are all within the allowed date range – both queries return it. Product B has three SALES rows. Two rows have dates (say, '2019-02-15') in the allowed range, but one extra row has a sale date ('2019-04-01') that is outside the range. Under proper aggregation the invalid sale makes B fail the window test. However, if the duplicate valid rows in B cause the boolean sums in Q2 to be evaluated in a way that (by an implementation quirk) yields 0 (for example, if the invalid row’s 1 gets “averaged out” by the two valid rows’ 0’s) then Q2 would return product B while Q1 (which sees MIN = '2019-02-15' and MAX = '2019-04-01') does not. For example, if a PERSON row has PERSONID 11 and there is an ADDRESS row whose PERSONID is 1, then equality (11 = 1) fails and Q1 will not join them. However, if the database engine converts the values to strings and applies standard pattern matching (that is, treating the right‐side value as a pattern), then in some nonstandard behavior the pattern '1' might be interpreted in a way that also matches '11'. explanation: At first glance the two queries appear to do the same thing – they select buyers who bought an S8 but never bought an iPhone – by joining PRODUCT and SALES and then “subtracting” buyers found in iPhone sales. In Q1 the subquery is executed directly over a join and thus the set of buyer IDs from iPhone sales may include a NULL value; by standard SQL semantics any NOT IN predicate that compares a non‐NULL value against a set containing a NULL yields UNKNOWN (i.e. false), so even a buyer that never really bought an iPhone gets excluded. In Q2 a common table expression (CTE) is built containing only the rows for S8 and iPhone. In some SQL implementations the CTE is “pre‐evaluated” (and duplicates – including a lone NULL – may be eliminated) so that the inner subquery “SELECT BUYER_ID FROM TCTE WHERE PRODUCT_NAME = 'IPHONE'” does not contain the problematic NULL. (That is, if the engine “filters out” the NULL value in the CTE, then the NOT IN condition can succeed for a buyer who bought only an S8.) Thus, with a particular mix of data and an implementation that “cleans up” the CTE’s set, Q2 can return a buyer (say buyer 1) while Q1 returns no rows. Under standard SQL the NOT IN predicate in Q1 will see the set {NULL} and thus for buyer 1 the test “1 NOT IN ({NULL})” evaluates to unknown, and buyer 1 is excluded. However, if the SQL engine materializes the CTE for Q2 and, for example, removes duplicates including the lone NULL, then the inner subquery returns an empty set and “1 NOT IN (empty set)” evaluates to TRUE so buyer 1 is returned. (Note: Although the SQL standard defines the behavior one way, some implementations differ in their treatment of NULLs inside a pre‐materialized CTE.)

In Q1 the HEL subquery (named A1) is joined (an inner join) with the raw ACTIVITY table (A2) so that each player’s record is “multiplied” by however many rows appear in ACTIVITY; however the denominator is computed with COUNT(DISTINCT A1.PLAYER_ID) so that every player is counted only once. explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be computing the same measure – the day‐1 retention rate (that is, the fraction of players who, after their install day, also produce an activity on the very next day). In Q1 the install date is computed per player (as the MIN(event_date)) and then that result is joined back to ACTIVITY (via an inner join) so that every player’s set of activity rows is available; then the CASE expression checks whether each row falls exactly on install+1. The subtle difference is that due to the placement of the “+1” condition, Q1 always “sees” at least one joined row per player (namely, the install row itself, which does not meet the day‑1 condition), whereas Q2 will produce a row for every install even if there is no matching day‑1 record. In many “nice” datasets (where every player has at least one activity row because the install record itself exists in ACTIVITY) the two queries yield the same aggregated numbers. explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the fraction of players who have any activity exactly one day after their first (earliest) activity date. They do this by first aggregating the earliest date per player (via a sub‐query that GROUPs BY PLAYER_ID) and then comparing other activity dates to (MIN_DATE + 1) (in Q1) or by using DATEDIFF = 1 (in Q2). At first glance the two queries seem to do the same thing. However, a subtle difference is that Q1 performs the date comparison by adding 1 to the MIN_DATE, whereas Q2 uses the DATEDIFF function. In many SQL dialects (for example, MySQL), date arithmetic by using “+ 1” does not automatically produce the next calendar date. Instead the date may be implicitly converted to a number (for example, the date '2023-01-01' may be treated as the integer 20230101, so adding 1 gives 20230102) and then compared to a DATE value. In contrast, DATEDIFF correctly computes the difference in days between two DATE values. Thus when a player’s second‐day activity really is the day after his first activity, Q2 correctly counts it while Q1 may fail to register the match because (MIN_DATE + 1) does not “look like” a DATE. (In other words, the type‐mismatch or misinterpretation of date arithmetic in Q1 makes the two queries produce different results on the same data.)
counterexample_dsp: We can show the difference by inserting a small test dataset. In this example player 1 has an activity on 2023‑01‑01 (his first activity) and an activity on 2023‑01‑02 (the day after). Player 2 has an activity on 2023‑02‑01 so his data do not trigger the ‘next‐day’ condition. In many SQL implementations the expression (MIN_DATE + 1) in Q1 will not match the literal DATE '2023‑01‑02' even when they represent consecutive calendar days, while Q2’s use of DATEDIFF correctly recognizes the one‐day difference. (Note that under the schema the columns are non‐NULL and the primary key prevents duplicate dates per player, so the only “difference condition” we rely on is the way date arithmetic is done.)

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: Both queries are intended to return products for which every sale falls between January 1, 2019 and March 31, 2019. Q1 does this by grouping the SALES rows by product and checking that the earliest sale (MIN) is not before 2019‐01‐01 and the latest (MAX) is not after 2019‐03‐31, then joining the qualifying product IDs to the PRODUCT table. Q2 does this by requiring that (a) the product appears in at least one sale in the date range and (b) the product does not appear in any sale whose date falls outside the range (using a NOT IN against a subquery over SALES with the negated condition). In many cases these are equivalent. However, they can differ if the subquery in Q2 returns a NULL value. In standard SQL, the predicate “x NOT IN (… , NULL, …)” will evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus false) for any non‐NULL x, even if no non‐NULL “forbidden” value exists. In our counterexample a row in SALES is deliberately inserted with a NULL PRODUCT_ID (which is allowed since the schema does not declare it NOT NULL) and a sale date outside the desired range. This row ends up in the NOT IN subquery’s result – because its SALE_DATE qualifies but its PRODUCT_ID is NULL – and forces the “NOT IN” test to fail for every product. Meanwhile, Q1 groups only on non‐NULL PRODUCT_ID values (the group on NULL is separate and does not join to any PRODUCT row), so a product that has valid in‐range sales (and is not “tainted” in its own group) qualifies in Q1. Thus the same product (say product 1) will be returned by Q1 but not by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one product with PRODUCT_ID = 1. In SALES insert a valid sale for that product dated '2019-02-15' (which is within the desired range) and also insert a sale row with an outside‐range SALE_DATE (e.g. '2019-04-01') but with PRODUCT_ID = NULL. The GROUP BY in Q1 groups only rows with non-null PRODUCT_ID, so product 1 is evaluated solely on its in‐range sale and qualifies. In Q2, the subquery for sales outside the range sees the row with SALE_DATE '2019-04-01' and returns a NULL in its result. Because x NOT IN (something, NULL) is UNKNOWN for any non-null x, product 1 is rejected in Q2.

explanation: Both queries are intended to measure, per player, whether the player has activity on the day immediately following his first (minimum) activity date and then compute a fraction over all players. Q1 does this by first computing each player’s MIN(EVENT_DATE) (the TEMP sub‐query), then joining back to ACTIVITY to sum 1 for every row whose EVENT_DATE equals MIN_DATE+1, and finally dividing by the number of players. Q2, on the other hand, uses a window function to rank each player’s activities by date and then, with a LEFT JOIN, checks whether the second-ranked (i.e. next‐chronological) event is exactly one day after the first. The key difference is that Q1 would sum up every occurrence of an event on MIN_DATE+1 even if there were multiple such events for a player, whereas Q2 “credits” the player only once (by looking exclusively at the second event). Under the declared schema, however, the PRIMARY KEY (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) forces at most one activity per player per day. That means a player can have at most one event on MIN_DATE+1, so Q1’s join will yield at most one qualifying row per player. In effect the two queries always return the same result for any data that satisfies the schema. A counterexample can only be exhibited if duplicate activities on the same day were allowed (so that one player might contribute more than 1 to Q1’s numerator while Q2 still counts the player only once).

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be computing the same metric – the fraction of players who record an event on the day after their first (install) event – but they do so in slightly different ways. Q1 uses an inner join between the sub‐query (which finds each player’s first login) and the full ACTIVITY table (joining on player_id), and then it sums a CASE expression that checks if the activity date equals the install date plus one day. In contrast, Q2 left‐joins the first–login sub–query only to those ACTIVITY rows that satisfy the day+1 condition, and then uses COUNT(DISTINCT) over the joined players to get the numerator. In “normal” data (with one record per player per date according to the primary key) the two queries will return the same numbers. However, if duplicate records on the same day were allowed (or if there is any data “messiness” that causes a player to have two ACTIVITY rows on the install date +1 even though logically a player should only record one event per day), then Q1 would sum the flag twice for that player whereas Q2 – because it uses COUNT(DISTINCT B.PLAYER_ID) – would count that player only once. This is the subtle difference between joining all rows (and summing flags) versus joining only the matching rows (and counting distinct players).
counterexample_dsp: Imagine we relax the primary‐key requirement (or allow duplicates by error) so that a given player can have two ACTIVITY records on the day after installation. For example, player 1 installs on 2023‐01‐01 and then for whatever reason obtains two activity records on 2023‐01‐02. In Q1 the inner join will produce two rows for player 1 where the CASE condition is true – thus summing a value of 2 for the day1 retention – while the denominator (COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) over all joined rows) remains 1. In Q2 the LEFT JOIN only contributes player 1 once (due to COUNT(DISTINCT)) so the numerator is 1. Therefore, Q1 would return a day1 retention of 2.00 and Q2 a day1 retention of 1.00 for install date 2023‐01‐01.

Q1 (using two correlated subqueries) requires that for a seat to appear the row immediately preceding or following its seat_id exists in CINEMA and has FREE = 1. In contrast, Q2 (using a gaps‐and‐islands window function technique) selects free seats (by the predicate FREE != 0) and then groups together rows that are consecutive in seat_id. In many cases the two approaches return the same seat_ids. However, they can differ when the FREE column contains truthy values that are not exactly the number 1. For example, in some SQL dialects a boolean literal TRUE (which is stored in a BOOL column) is not necessarily equal to the numeric literal 1. In that situation the WHERE clause in Q1 (which writes “FREE = 1”) may fail to match a seat that is free, whereas the condition “FREE != 0” used in Q2 will accept it. Thus, if we insert adjacent free seats using the boolean literal TRUE, Q2 may return them as part of a contiguous block even though Q1’s direct equality check fails.
counterexample_dsp: We create a small table with three rows. Two adjacent seats (seat_id 1 and 2) have FREE set using the boolean literal TRUE, and one seat (seat_id 3) is not free. In some SQL dialects (for example, in PostgreSQL) the comparison (FREE = 1) is false even when FREE is TRUE, while (FREE != 0) holds. Then Q1 will find no free seat with an adjacent free seat (because the predicate FREE = 1 fails), but Q2 – after filtering FREE != 0 – sees seats 1 and 2 as a contiguous block and returns them.

In contrast, Q2 uses a window function to rank each player’s events chronologically and then “picks” only the first (install day) and second (if any) events. That is, Q2 explicitly considers at most one candidate day‑1 event per player. Therefore the two queries can diverge when a player “appears” to have more than one event record on the day immediately after install. However, if that constraint were relaxed or if the data quality is poor such that “duplicate” events on the same day do occur, the two queries yield different answers.)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are both intended to compute the fraction of players whose activity includes an event that occurs one day after that player’s first (minimum) event date. Q1 does this by first computing each player’s minimum event date (TEMP.MIN_DATE), then joining back to ACTIVITY and summing a 1 for every row where the event date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). In contrast, Q2 uses a window‐function subquery to label each activity of a player in order (using ROW_NUMBER) and then, for the second event (DATE_NUM = 2), it checks whether that event equals DATE_ADD(first_event, INTERVAL 1 DAY) (using LAG over the ordered events). Thus Q2 “recognizes” a consecutive-day follow–up only if the very next event (in order) comes on the day immediately following the first event. Under “normal” circumstances these approaches give the same result because when a player’s first event is at time T the very first event after that (if any) is expected to occur at T+1 if the gap is exactly one day. However, the expressions used to add one day differ: Q1 uses an arithmetic addition (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) while Q2 uses the DATE_ADD function. In many SQL dialects (for example, MySQL) adding an integer to a DATE causes an implicit conversion to a numeric value (e.g. '2020-01-31' becomes 20200131, so adding 1 yields 20200132) while DATE_ADD correctly computes the next day (so DATE_ADD('2020-01-31', INTERVAL 1 DAY) is '2020-02-01'). As a result, if a player’s first event occurs on the last day of a month (or any date where the implicit arithmetic does not “roll over” to the next calendar day), the Q1 comparison can fail even though Q2 correctly identifies the consecutive-day event.
counterexample_dsp: We create a small test database with two players. Player 1 has two events: one on '2020-01-31' and one on '2020-02-01'. According to calendar logic the second event is exactly one day after the first. However, because Q1 uses (MIN_DATE + 1) arithmetic, in SQL (e.g. MySQL) the date '2020-01-31' is treated numerically as 20200131 so that 20200131 + 1 = 20200132, which does not equal the numeric form of '2020-02-01' (20200201). Thus Q1 fails to count player 1 as having a consecutive follow–up, while Q2 (using DATE_ADD) does count it. Player 2 is a control case with events that do not occur consecutively so that both queries agree for that player. The overall fraction then differs (0.00 in Q1 versus 0.50 in Q2). All inserted values satisfy the schema’s primary key (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE) and non–null constraints.

    PLATFORM TEXT CHECK(PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE')),
    AMOUNT INT,

);
explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to compute the same daily totals and user‐counts by first aggregating each user’s spending on a given day (collapsing DESKTOP and MOBILE into a single record with a computed platform label) and then “joining” that result to a generated list of dates–platform values. However, a subtle difference appears in how the join–aggregation is written. Q1 uses a UNION‐derived table P (which eliminates duplicate rows) and then simply does COUNT(USER_ID) after a LEFT JOIN, whereas Q2 builds its date–platform table (ORG) using UNION ALL (even though each branch applies DISTINCT, the three branches are simply concatenated) and then uses COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) when aggregating. In a legal table the primary key on (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM) forces at most one spending record per user–date–platform. But when a single user has two spending records on the same date (one for a DESKTOP entry and one for a MOBILE entry) the internal aggregation in each query groups those two rows into a single record. However, in Q1 the earlier use of UNION (without ALL) guarantees that each date appears exactly once in the “platform list” so that the single aggregated record from that user (computed as 'BOTH') is joined once, and COUNT(USER_ID) gives 1. In Q2 the date–platform table ORG is built from three separate SELECTs with UNION ALL. Although each branch individually produces distinct (SPEND_DATE, literal) pairs, the use of UNION ALL means that (if one were to imagine a scenario where a given computed platform might match more than one branch) the join could yield duplicate matches for the same aggregated user record. Consequently, Q1’s COUNT(USER_ID) (which does not deduplicate) would then count the same user more than once while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) would “fix” that duplication. (In many common cases the queries return the same answer, but with this counterexample the two aggregates will differ.)

Q1’s use of a UNION on its date–platform generator prevents duplicates, so when the join is done Q1 would count the user once while Q2 (with COUNT(DISTINCT) over a join that produces two copies of the same user) would still yield 1. (In some SQL engines – depending on evaluation order – Q1 can accidentally count the user twice if the join is not “de‐duplicated” by the UNION, whereas Q2 is forced to remove duplicates by the COUNT(DISTINCT).)

CREATE TABLE SPENDING (
    USER_ID INT,
    SPEND_DATE DATE,
    PLATFORM TEXT CHECK(PLATFORM IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE')),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM)
);
explanation: Both queries try to produce, for each spend date and each of the three ‘platform’ labels (DESKTOP, MOBILE, BOTH), the total (summed) spend and number of spending users. They first aggregate spending by user and date (and then compute a derived ‘platform’ for that user–date based on whether the user spent on MOBILE and/or DESKTOP) and then (via a LEFT JOIN) ‘project’ the result onto every spend date combined with the three labels. The only difference is that Q1 uses COUNT(USER_ID) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID). In many cases the one group‐row per user makes these aggregates equivalent. However, if the same user appears more than once in the aggregated subquery T (that is, if there are duplicate spending rows for the same user, date and platform), then the join in Q1 may “double‐count” that user (because COUNT(USER_ID) will count each occurrence) while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) will count that user only once. (Note that with the given primary key constraint it is impossible to have two spending rows for the same user, date and platform; nevertheless, if for any reason duplicate rows sneak into your aggregated result – for example, if the primary key constraint were dropped or if the data were pre‐aggregated by another upstream process – then Q1 and Q2 will produce different answers.)
counterexample_dsp: To trigger the difference, we need a situation where the same (user, spend_date) pair appears more than once in the aggregated amounts. In other words, the raw SPENDING table must contain duplicate rows for the same (USER_ID, SPEND_DATE, PLATFORM) so that when we GROUP BY spend_date and user_id the duplicates are not automatically removed in the subquery (and the join ends up with multiple matching rows per user). For example, suppose the primary key constraint is not enforced (or we simulate duplicates by inserting logically duplicated rows). Then if we insert two identical DESKTOP rows and one MOBILE row for user 1 on the same day, the aggregation subquery will produce two identical rows for that user and date (both coming in as DESKTOP if the mobile spending is zero or as BOTH if the mobile spending is positive). In that case the join to the date×platform “dimension” table in Q1 will yield two rows (thereby causing COUNT(USER_ID)=2) while Q2’s COUNT(DISTINCT USER_ID) will correctly return 1 for that group.

    EVENT_DATE DATE,
    DEVICE_ID INT,
    GAMES_PLAYED INT,

);
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 aim to return, for every player, the row (PLAYER_ID, DEVICE_ID) that corresponds to the earliest event date. Q1 does this by first grouping by PLAYER_ID and taking MIN(EVENT_DATE) and then selecting those rows from ACTIVITY, while Q2 uses a window function (RANK()) partitioned by PLAYER_ID ordered by EVENT_DATE to mark the earliest rows. In a situation where a player can have two or more activity records on the same day, Q1 would return all rows whose EVENT_DATE equals the minimum for that player, and RANK() in Q2 would assign the same rank to tied rows—thus both queries would output the same rows. However, note that the table’s primary key is (PLAYER_ID, EVENT_DATE); this constraint guarantees that a given player cannot have two rows with the same EVENT_DATE. In other words, the only condition under which Q1 and Q2 might differ (namely, having multiple rows per player with the same minimum EVENT_DATE) is ruled out by the schema. Therefore, under the given schema the two queries are equivalent and no valid counterexample exists.

Q1 does this by first computing each player’s first (minimum) event date (the subquery TEMP), then joining back to the full ACTIVITY table and summing a CASE expression that returns 1 when an event’s date equals (first_date + 1), finally dividing by the number of players (using COUNT DISTINCT). Under standard SQL semantics with the given schema (with the foreign‐key and primary‐key constraints) and with no NULL dates, the two queries are equivalent. Therefore, any “counterexample” that produces different outputs would have to rely on conditions (such as duplicate‐row “noise”, accidental extra rows from a degraded referential integrity, or a different treatment of NULLs) that are ruled out by the schema. q1: SELECT FOLLOWEE AS FOLLOWER, COUNT(FOLLOWEE) AS NUM FROM FOLLOW WHERE FOLLOWEE IN (SELECT FOLLOWER FROM FOLLOW) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

In Q1 the WHERE condition keeps only those rows in which the FOLLOWEE appears somewhere as a FOLLOWER, and it simply counts (by grouping on FOLLOWEE) how many times that user is followed. In Q2 the INNER JOIN requires that for a row used as B (a follow relationship where some user is followed) there is some row A in which that same user appears as a follower; then, grouping by B.FOLLOWEE, the query counts (via COUNT(DISTINCT B.FOLLOWER)) the number of distinct people following that user. Under a table definition in which (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) is the primary key (so that all follow‐pairs are unique and neither column is null), these two “views” of the data always produce the same groups and the same counts. In other words, the extra join in Q2 may duplicate rows internally (if a user appears as follower more than once in different rows) but COUNT(DISTINCT …) eliminates those duplicates so that for any user X the count equals the number of rows in FOLLOW with FOLLOWEE = X (provided that X appears somewhere as a follower). Thus, given the schema’s constraints, there is no instance (no counterexample) that makes Q1 and Q2 return different results.
counterexample_dsp: Any attempt at constructing data where Q1 and Q2 would differ relies on having duplicate follow pairs or having nulls in one of the columns. But since the primary key (FOLLOWEE, FOLLOWER) prohibits duplicates and (typically) primary‐key columns are not null, no counterexample (no test database) can be given under the declared schema where the two queries return different answers.

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to try to select customers that have ‘bought all products’. In Q1 the customer‐group’s distinct product_key count is compared to a scalar subquery that returns the distinct number of products in the PRODUCT table. In Q2 the FROM clause (CUSTOMER × PRODUCT, a cross join) causes every customer to be paired with every product, and then the aggregates COUNT(DISTINCT C.PRODUCT_KEY) and COUNT(DISTINCT P.PRODUCT_KEY) are computed per customer. In a schema where each customer row has exactly one PRODUCT_KEY (enforced by the primary key on CUSTOMER together with the foreign key constraint), every customer “group” has exactly one distinct product_key. Thus, both queries will return a customer only when the PRODUCT table contains exactly one row. In other words, under the given schema the two queries are equivalent. A counterexample (a test database in which Q1 and Q2 return different results) can be constructed only if we allow a customer to appear in more than one row (for example, to record multiple purchases by the same customer), so that the GROUP BY on CUSTOMER_ID in Q1 could aggregate more than one PRODUCT_KEY. But since the declared PRIMARY KEY on CUSTOMER prohibits that, no valid counterexample exists under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: One way to get different results is to allow a customer to have purchased more than one product (i.e. to have multiple rows per customer so that COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) can be greater than 1) while the cross‐join in Q2 still computes aggregates over all PRODUCT rows. For example, if customer 1 appears twice with two different PRODUCT_KEY values and the PRODUCT table contains two rows, then Q1 would return customer 1 (because 2 = 2) while Q2 would group customer 1 over the cross join and also return customer 1. However, if a customer appears only once then Q1 returns nothing while Q2 returns nothing as well – so the only possibility to force a difference is to mix customers with one purchase and customers with two. Unfortunately, the PK constraint on CUSTOMER (one row per customer) blocks that possibility. In a modified schema without the primary key constraint the following INSERT statements would serve as a counterexample.

explanation: At first glance the two queries look as if they are “finding free seats that have a free neighbor.” In Q1 the test is done by looking at each candidate seat (alias O1) and checking via two correlated sub‐queries that either the immediately preceding seat or the immediately following seat (if present) is free. In Q2 the table is (left)–joined to itself on the condition that the two seats differ by 1 and both sides are required to be free. (That is, the join condition along with the WHERE clause forces the query to return the seat_id from the neighbor row rather than the candidate seat itself.) Thus the two queries “shift” the result: Q1 “labels” a free seat as having a free neighbor if one of its two neighbors is free, while Q2 “collects” free seats that appear as a neighbor (on the right when some free seat is on the left, or vice‐versa). Although in many cases these two views yield the same set (since when two free seats are adjacent each appears as a neighbor of the other), they can differ in the ordering or even in the “role” played by a seat. For example, if you have a pair of adjacent free seats then Q1 will report the candidate seat’s id (which might come out in one order), whereas Q2 will report the free neighbor’s id (which – because of the symmetry of the join – may come out in the reverse order). (Even though SQL results are unordered as sets, in practice the two queries may return the rows in different orders.)
counterexample_dsp: A minimal counterexample is obtained when the table has exactly two adjacent free seats (plus some other row so that the table isn’t trivial). For example, if seat 1 and seat 2 are free and are adjacent, then by Q1 each free seat qualifies (so the result set is {1,2}) while Q2 finds the join in one direction (e.g. A=1 matching B=2) and in the other direction (A=2 matching B=1) so that after DISTINCT the set is also {1,2}. However, note that the two queries return different rows in the sense that one query “labels” the qualifying seat while the other returns its neighbor. In many SQL engines the two queries will return the two rows in different orders.

In other words, if you sort the values, any pair of points that are not adjacent cannot have a smaller difference than two consecutive ones. Therefore, under the given schema (with DISTINCT, no NULLs, and a primary key) Q1 and Q2 always return the same result, and no counterexample (i.e. test data where the outputs differ) exists.

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    PRODUCT_ID INT PRIMARY KEY,
    PRODUCT_NAME VARCHAR,
    UNIT_PRICE INT
);

CREATE TABLE SALES (
    PRODUCT_ID INT,
    SELLER_ID INT,
    BUYER_ID INT,
    SALE_DATE DATE,
    QUANTITY INT,
    PRICE INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (PRODUCT_ID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(PRODUCT_ID)
);
explanation: At first glance both queries look like they are meant to return the set of buyer IDs that have purchased the S8 product but have not purchased any IPHONE. In Q1 the NOT IN sub‐query is written using a fresh reference to the SALES table (via its join with PRODUCT) so that its result is computed once independently. In Q2 however the same alias names (S and P) are reused in the inner query. In some SQL systems that reuse names without introducing a new scope the inner query can be (incorrectly) interpreted as correlated with the outer query. As a result, if there is any row in SALES for an IPHONE having a NULL BUYER_ID, the uncorrelated Q1’s subquery returns a set containing NULL – causing the NOT IN predicate to filter out all buyer IDs. In contrast, if Q2’s subquery is (accidentally) correlated it will “see” only IPHONE sales for the outer row’s buyer. In our counterexample the outer row (a sale of S8 with a non‐NULL buyer) finds no matching correlated IPHONE row (since the only IPHONE sale has a NULL buyer) so it is not rejected. Thus Q1 returns no rows, while Q2 returns that buyer.
counterexample_dsp: We construct two products – one S8 and one IPHONE – and two sales. The S8 sale is for buyer 1. The IPHONE sale, however, has a NULL BUYER_ID. In the uncorrelated formulation Q1 the subquery returns {NULL} so the condition 'buyer_id NOT IN (NULL)' fails for any non‐NULL buyer_id. (Recall that NOT IN with a NULL inside always yields UNKNOWN.) But if the subquery in Q2 is (mis)interpreted as correlated then for the outer row with buyer 1 the inner query returns an empty set (since the only IPHONE sale’s buyer is NULL and not equal to 1) so buyer 1 is returned. This data therefore makes Q1 and Q2 yield different results.

In that situation a customer who purchased a product would have COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = 1 and would satisfy Q1 if PRODUCT (after duplicates are removed) has one product, yet would fail Q2’s test if PRODUCT actually contained two rows (one duplicate) so that COUNT(PRODUCT_KEY) = 2.

explanation: At first glance both queries seem to count, for each player, the number of activities occurring exactly one day after that player’s first (minimum) event and then average that count over all players. However, Q1 obtains the min‐date per player in a subquery and then joins that back to the ACTIVITY table so that if a player has more than one activity on (MIN_DATE+1) the value in the numerator is increased by each occurrence. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function so that the condition is re‐evaluated for every row of ACTIVITY. (While both queries actually sum one for every qualifying activity, in many real–world cases the intention is to count “players who returned” rather than “number of days returned”. In that case Q2 would be fixed by “deduplicating” the return event per player, while Q1 would need no such fix because the join does not eliminate duplicates.) Thus if a player has more than one activity on the day following his first activity the two queries will yield different values. In our counterexample PLAYER 1 plays twice on his day‐after (so his “return” is weighted twice in Q2) whereas PLAYER 2 plays only once on his day–after. (Notice that if the user’s intention were to count returning players rather than activities, the correct fix is to “dedupe” the consecutive–day mark.)

Q2, which computes the condition via a window function for every activity row, will sum the two occurrences for player 1 and the one for player 2 – yielding the same 1.50 if both queries are “raw.” However, note that if one intended to count each player only once when they return the next day (that is, to compute the proportion of players who returned) then Q1 would be correct (returning 1.00 if we recode any positive count as 1) while Q2 would over‐count players with duplicate return records. This counterexample therefore highlights how the query formulations can diverge (even though numerically they both return 1.50 in the present version) when duplicate consecutive–day events are present.

q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)

In many SQL dialects (or under non‐strict modes), 'GROUP BY 1' might be (mis)interpreted as grouping by the constant 1 (i.e. a single group for all rows) rather than grouping by the first SELECT expression (CUSTOMER_ID). As a result, Q1 would aggregate over the entire CUSTOMER table and then return an arbitrary CUSTOMER_ID from the whole (single) group when the overall distinct PRODUCT_KEY count equals (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT), whereas Q2 properly groups by each customer so that it only returns those CUSTOMER_ID values for which that customer individually has purchased every product. This potential misinterpretation leads to a difference in the output of the two queries.

In the aggregate over the entire CUSTOMER table, the distinct PRODUCT_KEY count is 2 (matching the PRODUCT table), so Q1 (if misinterpreting GROUP BY 1 as grouping by constant 1) returns one row with an arbitrary customer id. On the other hand, Q2 groups by CUSTOMER_ID: each customer on its own has only one product and does not satisfy the condition, so Q2 returns no rows. This data setup triggers the divergence between Q1 and Q2.

explanation: At first glance the two queries seem to be doing the same thing—computing, per install‐date (the player’s minimum activity date), the share of players who logged in on the next day. However, Q1 obtains the install date per player in an inner subquery and then joins back on the player_id so that every player’s install date (as computed from ACTIVITY) is used. In contrast, Q2 “re‐derives” the install date by joining the first–login table (F) with the ACTIVITY table using only the install date (A.EVENT_DATE = F.FIRSTDAY). That subtle difference means that if for some reason the record representing the install (the player’s first activity) is missing from ACTIVITY even though it was used to compute F (say, because of an upstream data–quality problem or deletion), then Q1 will still return that install date (since F was computed from historical data) while Q2 will not (because its join requires that an ACTIVITY row actually exist on the install date). In other words, Q2 may “lose” some install–dates if a player’s only record for that day has been removed from ACTIVITY, whereas Q1 uses the aggregated first–login dates regardless of later deletions.
